title: Maximum Value Sum by Placing Three Rooks II
statement:
`board` is an `m x n` grid of integers, and `board[i][j]` is the value written on cell `(i, j)`. Put exactly three rooks on the board so that no two of them sit in the same row or in the same column (a shared row or column would let them attack each other). Return the largest possible sum of the values under the three rooks.

All three rooks must be placed, even when every value is negative.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every triple of cells costs O((m · n)^3), hopeless on a 500 × 500 board. Instead, order the rooks by row and fix the middle one, in row `mid`. The upper rook is above `mid` and the lower one below it, so rows never clash; only columns can.

The upper rook must avoid at most two columns, those of the other rooks. So above `mid` we only need each column's best value and the three best columns: one of them always survives, and it is at least as good as any blocked choice. The same holds below `mid`, and the middle rook simply tries every column of its row.

## Approach

1. `bestThree(colBest)` returns the three `[value, column]` pairs with the largest values: it pushes each column into a short list, sorts it, and drops a fourth entry.
2. Sweep rows upward from the bottom: `colBelow[col]` is the best value of that column from `row` down, and `below[row] = bestThree(colBelow)`.
3. Sweep `mid` from row 1 to row `m - 2`, folding row `mid - 1` into `colAbove` and computing `above`.
4. For every cell of row `mid`, try the 3 × 3 pairs from `above` and `below[mid + 1]`; when all three columns differ, update `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

Only `mid = 1` exists. Row 0 `[-3, 1, 1, 1]` gives `above = [[1, 1], [1, 2], [1, 3]]`, and row 2 `[-3, 2, 1, 1]` gives `below[2] = [[2, 1], [1, 2], [1, 3]]`. With the middle rook in column 3 (value 1), the upper rook in column 2 and the lower rook in column 1 give `1 + 1 + 2 = 4`, and no other combination beats it.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n): each row updates one column array and calls `bestThree` once (sorting at most four pairs per step), and each middle cell tries 9 pairs.
- Space: O(m + n) for the column arrays and three pairs per row in `below`.

## Pitfalls

- Keeping only the single best column above or below fails when the middle rook needs that column; two columns can be blocked, so keep three.
- Rank columns by their best value, not the three largest cells overall: those cells might share a column.
- Start `best` at `-Infinity`, because the answer can be negative.
- A sum can reach 3 · 10^9, beyond a 32-bit integer, hence the `long` result.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `m`, `n` | number of rows and columns |
| `bestThree` | the three `[value, column]` pairs with the largest values |
| `colBelow`, `colAbove` | best value of each column below, or above, the middle row |
| `below[row]` | the three best columns over rows `row..m - 1` |
| `mid` | the middle rook's row |
| `above` | the three best columns over rows `0..mid - 1` |
| `upValue`, `upCol` / `downValue`, `downCol` | the candidate upper and lower rooks |
| `best` | the largest sum found so far |
